quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Every morning at 7:15, the old tram on Bridge Street clatters past the bakery, the pharmacy, and the school. Passengers know each other by sight and nod as they board. When the city announced a plan to replace it with a faster line underground, a petition to keep the tram gathered four thousand names in a week. It seems that what people would lose is more than a way to get downtown.
options: A Petition Signed by Four Thousand
Plans for a Faster Underground Line
The Meaning of an Old Tram to Its Riders
quests.correctAnswer: The Meaning of an Old Tram to Its Riders
quests.hint: The passage never says why people signed. What do the details about the passengers suggest?
quests.explanation: The petition is evidence, and the underground plan is the trigger. The nodding passengers and the closing sentence point to the tram's value beyond transport.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title draws together the daily routine, the familiar faces, and the petition to show what the tram means to the community.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: At the back of the classroom, one desk is always kept clear. When Mr. Farid started teaching, an older colleague explained the tradition: it is for the student who arrives late, embarrassed, and afraid of being noticed. The desk sits by the door, away from the board, so a latecomer can slip in without stopping the lesson. No one has ever mentioned it aloud, but Mr. Farid says the quiet welcome has kept several students from giving up.
options: A Teacher's First Week at School
Why Students Arrive Late to Class
quests.correctAnswer: Quietly Welcoming Latecomers
quests.hint: Ask what the empty desk is meant to do, not just where it is.
quests.explanation: The seat's position is a detail, and lateness is only the situation. The passage is about the kindness that the arrangement quietly offers.
quests.whyThisTitle: It captures the purpose behind the reserved desk: welcoming students without drawing attention to them.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When Nadia opened a shop for paper maps, friends thought she was joking. Phones already gave directions. But her customers turned out to be hikers who lose signal in the mountains, sailors who like a backup, and travelers who enjoy seeing a whole region at once instead of a single blue dot. Sales have grown every year since.
options: Opening a Shop Against Friends' Advice
quests.correctAnswer: Paper Maps Still Finding Buyers
quests.hint: The passage begins with doubt. How does it end?
quests.explanation: The hikers are one group of customers, and the friends' doubt is only the opening. The passage as a whole explains why there is still demand.
quests.whyThisTitle: The three kinds of customers together explain why the shop succeeded despite the doubts.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The log of an old lighthouse records the weather each day in the same plain words: 'wind north, sea calm, no ships.' For thirty years the entries barely change. Then one page reads: 'Fog. Sounded the horn all night.' Below it, in the margin, someone has added a single line: 'Nine boats came home.'
options: Weather Records from an Old Lighthouse
One Night That Justified the Routine
quests.correctAnswer: One Night That Justified the Routine
quests.hint: Compare the thirty repetitive years with the one page that is different.
quests.explanation: The weather notes and the boats are both details. The contrast between years of sameness and one important night carries the meaning.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title joins the long routine to the single night that showed why it mattered.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The finance team received a new invoicing program last spring, with a two-day training session and a manual of two hundred pages. Six weeks later, most people were still using the old spreadsheets. Only when a colleague made a short video showing the three tasks everyone did daily did the new program begin to catch on. The training, it seems, had explained everything except what mattered to the people using it.
options: Why Training Missed What Users Needed
A Two-Hundred-Page Manual for New Software
quests.correctAnswer: Why Training Missed What Users Needed
quests.hint: Look at what worked in the end and what that says about what failed.
quests.explanation: The manual and the spreadsheets are part of the story. The final sentence says the real problem was the mismatch between the training and the users' daily tasks.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title reflects the conclusion that the training was thorough but did not address what users actually did.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Nobody in the family gardens except Grandpa, and nobody quite understands why he spends every evening kneeling among the beans. His children buy vegetables from the market; the grandchildren find the soil boring. Yet every summer Sunday, the whole family arrives early, sits in the shade, and waits for him to bring out a basket. They come for the tomatoes, they say, but they stay for hours.
options: How a Garden Gathers a Family
quests.correctAnswer: How a Garden Gathers a Family
quests.hint: Notice the difference between the reason the family gives and how long they stay.
quests.explanation: The beans and the tomatoes are only the garden's contents. The last sentence shows that the family's real motive is being together.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice brings out what the family's Sunday visits show: the garden is the reason they gather.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Visitors to the museum's new exhibit often stop speaking as they enter the first room. It contains no glass cases or paintings, only a wall of ordinary shoes, thousands of them, collected from a single town after a flood. Labels are brief; there is no argument, no instruction, just the number of pairs and the date. Many leave without saying much, but few leave unmoved.
options: Rules for Behaving in a Museum
A Flood in a Small Town
quests.correctAnswer: The Power of Ordinary Objects
quests.hint: What creates the effect on the visitors: explanations, or something else?
quests.explanation: The flood and the shoe collection are facts inside the exhibit. The passage stresses that plain objects and short labels are enough to affect people.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title expresses how the plain display moves visitors without any commentary.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When the airline announced a four-hour delay, most passengers sighed and reached for their phones. One traveler, however, approached the desk with a suggestion: use the waiting time for a short talk about the city's history, since the airline had a guide on staff for special visitors. Within minutes, forty people were gathered near the gate. The delay did not shorten, but the mood did change.
options: Why Flights Are So Often Delayed
Turning a Flight Delay into an Opportunity
quests.correctAnswer: Turning a Flight Delay into an Opportunity
quests.hint: Compare the mood at the beginning with the mood at the end.
quests.explanation: Sighing passengers and the staff guide are details in the sequence. The passage shows a bad situation being improved by a suggestion.
quests.whyThisTitle: It captures the shift from frustration to engagement that a single idea produced.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Mr. Danjuma greets every passenger who boards his bus with the same phrase: 'Good to see you.' Some ignore him; some grumble. After a few months, though, the front seats fill first, riders begin greeting each other, and complaints about delays have dropped. The buses run no faster than before.
options: How a Simple Greeting Changed the Mood on a Bus
quests.correctAnswer: How a Simple Greeting Changed the Mood on a Bus
quests.hint: Look at how the last sentence rules something out. What does that leave as the cause of the change?
quests.explanation: Delays and complaints are aspects of the setting. Because the buses are no faster, the change must come from the greeting.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title ties the driver's repeated greeting to the friendlier atmosphere the passage describes.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: For months, Yara avoided speaking Spanish in front of others. She read well and understood almost everything, but she was afraid of a wrong verb ending. At last she joined a conversation group where everybody made mistakes and laughed about them. Within a month, her speaking had improved more than in the entire previous year. She had not learned new grammar; she had stopped being afraid.
options: Fear Rather Than Grammar Held Yara Back
quests.correctAnswer: Fear Rather Than Grammar Held Yara Back
quests.hint: The last sentence contains a contrast. Which idea does it correct?
quests.explanation: The conversation group is what changed things, but the passage is really about what the problem was. It says the obstacle was fear rather than knowledge.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title states the real obstacle that the passage uncovers in its final sentence.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The council planned to rename the road after a famous general, but residents objected. Long before the general was born, the road had been called Baker's Lane, after the family who sold bread from a cart along it. Older residents remembered the smell of the ovens; younger ones knew the name from wedding invitations and old photographs. In the end, the council kept the old name and placed a small plaque telling the general's story elsewhere.
options: Residents Fighting to Keep a Road's Old Name
A General Honored by the Council
The History of Bread in the Town
quests.correctAnswer: Residents Fighting to Keep a Road's Old Name
quests.hint: Ask why the residents cared, using the details about older and younger people.
quests.explanation: The general and the plaque are parts of the council's side. The memories and photographs show why the name had meaning for residents.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice pulls together the objection, the reasons behind it, and the result.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The coach watched her team lose a close game and, on the bus home, asked the players not what went wrong on the field but how they felt. Some were angry, others tired; she said little. At the next practice she changed nothing in the drills but began each session with a brief check-in. By season's end, the team's results were unchanged, yet no player had quit, which had been a problem in earlier years.
options: A Close Loss on the Sports Field
quests.correctAnswer: Check-Ins Instead of New Drills
quests.hint: Results did not change. What did?
quests.explanation: The loss starts the story, and the unchanged drills are a contrast. The coach's focus on feelings, and its effect on retention, is the real subject.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title shows what she changed and the outcome that mattered: players staying on the team.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The village schoolteacher used to correct children who dropped the endings of words, believing that a proper accent would help them find jobs. Decades later, researchers recorded the elders speaking the same way and found grammar rules that no textbook described. Some schools in the region now ask children to record their grandparents. The way people talk, it turns out, is more than a set of errors.
options: Rethinking the Value of Local Speech
quests.correctAnswer: Rethinking the Value of Local Speech
quests.hint: Follow how the teacher's belief at the start compares with what the researchers and schools do at the end.
quests.explanation: The teacher's belief, the research, and the school projects show a change of view. Each other title picks up only one step along the way.
quests.whyThisTitle: It reflects the shift from treating local speech as an error to valuing it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When Ravi's screen cracked, the shop near the station offered a repair for half the price of the authorized center. It worked well for six weeks; then the battery began to swell, and the new screen came loose. The authorized center explained that the cheaper shop had used parts not designed for his model. Ravi ended up paying more than if he had chosen the official repair from the start.
options: Choosing a Repair Shop Near the Station
When a Cheap Repair Costs More
quests.correctAnswer: When a Cheap Repair Costs More
quests.hint: Look at the final sentence. What was the outcome of the low price?
quests.explanation: The screen repair and the swollen battery are events in the story. The last sentence shows that the cheaper option cost more in the end.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title names the irony that the passage builds: a bargain that ended up costing more.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: For years, the neighbors Mrs. Liu and Mr. Adebayo argued about the fence between their gardens. One day a storm knocked it down, and neither seemed eager to rebuild it. Instead, Mr. Adebayo lent his ladder to help Mrs. Liu clear fallen branches, and she returned it with a jar of plum jam. The new fence went up months later, lower than the old one.
options: How a Storm Ended a Feud
quests.correctAnswer: How a Storm Ended a Feud
quests.hint: Which detail at the end hints that the relationship has changed?
quests.explanation: The jam and the fence are small events. The fact that the new fence is lower, and that neither hurries to rebuild, shows the quarrel has ended.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title links the storm, the shared help, and the lower fence as signs of a settled dispute.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A cookbook author once tested the same soup with three different amounts of salt and asked friends to taste them. Most preferred the middle one, but they could not explain why. The soup with too little salt tasted 'flat' and the one with too much tasted 'sharp,' though the other flavors were identical. The experiment showed how much a small ingredient can change our judgment of everything else on the plate.
options: How Salt Changes a Dish's Taste
A Guide to Choosing the Right Amount of Sugar
Making Soup for a Group of Friends
quests.correctAnswer: How Salt Changes a Dish's Taste
quests.hint: Consider what the experiment was designed to show.
quests.explanation: The soup and the friends are just the setup. The passage draws a conclusion about how one ingredient affects the taste of the rest.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice expresses the conclusion the experiment supports about salt's influence on overall flavor.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In some offices, a meeting begins with ten minutes of silent reading. Instead of listening to a presenter, everyone reads a short written memo and marks questions in the margin. Only afterward does the discussion start. Participants say the debate is calmer and more focused, because no one is reacting to half-formed ideas or the loudest voice.
quests.correctAnswer: How Silence Improves a Meeting
quests.hint: What do participants say the silence gives them?
quests.explanation: Memos, presenters, and loud voices all appear, but only as parts of the method or its contrast. The passage focuses on how the silent start changes the discussion.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title captures the link between the silent reading and the calmer, better discussion.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: While cleaning her attic, Leena found a photograph of a group of women in front of a sewing factory. On the back, someone had written a date and a list of names, but she recognized only one: her grandmother. Leena had always heard that her grandmother stayed at home. She began to ask relatives what else they had not been told.
options: The Photograph That Changed a Family Story
Recognizing Faces and Names from Long Ago
quests.correctAnswer: The Photograph That Changed a Family Story
quests.hint: Consider how the discovery affects what Leena believed before.
quests.explanation: The attic and the factory are only the setting of the discovery. The passage's turn is that the photograph contradicts what Leena had been told.
quests.whyThisTitle: It shows the effect of the discovery on Leena's understanding of her family.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Foxes now live in many large cities, and people often find them charming when they trot across quiet streets at night. But researchers have noticed changes. City foxes are bolder than their rural cousins, and some have learned to open trash cans. Others have grown less afraid of humans and even approach for food. Ecologists say this shows how quickly wild animals can adapt to human life.
options: Keeping Trash Cans Firmly Closed at Night
Feeding Wild Animals in City Parks
How City Life Is Changing Wild Foxes
quests.correctAnswer: How City Life Is Changing Wild Foxes
quests.hint: The passage starts with a pleasant image. Where does it end up?
quests.explanation: The opening scene and the trash cans are examples. The closing comment by ecologists sums up what the examples show.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title reflects the overall claim that urban living is altering fox behavior.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A company gave its employees free step counters, expecting healthier habits. In the first month, activity rose. Then, as the novelty faded, it dropped back below the earlier level, and some workers admitted to shaking the device to reach the target. The designers concluded that a gadget can start a habit but cannot sustain it without a personal reason to keep going.
options: Rising Activity in the First Month
Why a Step Counter Alone Did Not Change Habits
Cheating on a Daily Step Target
quests.correctAnswer: Why a Step Counter Alone Did Not Change Habits
quests.hint: Ask what the designers learned from the whole sequence, not just the first month.
quests.explanation: The free devices, the rise, and the cheating are steps in the story. The conclusion tells what the whole episode means.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title expresses the designers' conclusion that the device did not create lasting change.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The choir has no auditions. Anyone who turns up on Thursday evening in the church hall is given a folder and a place to stand. The singers include a retired judge, a taxi driver, and a girl who has just moved to the country. Their concerts are not flawless, but audiences often stay afterward to talk with performers, and singers say that between songs they have found friends they would never have met otherwise.
options: Meeting Friends in a Church Hall
quests.correctAnswer: Choir Where Anyone Can Belong
quests.hint: Which detail suggests what the choir values more than perfect singing?
quests.explanation: The imperfect concerts and the lack of auditions are both details. The passage's message is inclusion and friendship.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice captures the open membership and the friendships that the passage stresses.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When the bank redesigned its logo, customers complained, not about the look but about their cards. The new design meant every card had to be replaced, and many people distrusted emails asking them to 'confirm details' for the switch. Several fraud attempts followed. Analysts say the bank underestimated how a small visual change can disrupt trust, and it has since promised to notify customers by post first.
options: Choosing a New Design for the Company Logo
How a Logo Change Shook Customers' Trust
quests.correctAnswer: How a Logo Change Shook Customers' Trust
quests.hint: Which title covers the cause, the trouble, and the analysts' verdict?
quests.explanation: Card replacement and fraud are two effects of the change. The analysts' comment ties them into a single lesson about trust.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title unites the redesign, the confusion and fraud, and the bank's mistake about trust.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Volunteers at the river cleanup were surprised when the mayor arrived to thank them. Most had been coming every month for years and had never expected attention. One woman said she preferred the quiet mornings, when the only sounds were birds and the clink of glass in the buckets. When asked what kept her coming back, she pointed to the water: 'That's my thanks,' she said.
options: Volunteers Who Find Their Reward in the Work
A Mayor Arriving to Thank River Cleanup Volunteers
quests.correctAnswer: Volunteers Who Find Their Reward in the Work
quests.hint: Listen to what the woman says at the end. What does it say about the volunteers' motives?
quests.explanation: The mayor's visit and the sounds of the river are details. Her final answer explains what the volunteers value.
quests.whyThisTitle: It brings out the point of her reply: the cleaner river itself is what rewards them.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The dry cleaner on Market Street remembers everyone's clothes. He knows which customer likes a crease in her trousers, which one gets ink on his cuffs, and who is about to attend a wedding by the size of the garment bag. A younger competitor has an app that tracks orders, but customers say they do not feel recognized there. The old cleaner's business is not growing quickly, but it is not shrinking either.
options: Tracking Orders with a Phone App
The Strength of Personal Attention in a Small Business
quests.correctAnswer: The Strength of Personal Attention in a Small Business
quests.hint: Compare what each cleaner offers, and why customers stay.
quests.explanation: The app and the stains are details in a comparison. The passage suggests that personal recognition, not technology, is what keeps customers loyal.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title draws out the theme that knowing customers personally sustains the business.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Libraries were once places where visitors whispered under stern signs. Today, many have added a café, a games corner, and rooms where teenagers can practice music. Some readers complain that the noise is a betrayal of what a library is. Yet visit counts have doubled in cities that made these changes, and librarians report seeing people who had never come before.
options: The Library That Welcomes New Faces
quests.correctAnswer: The Library That Welcomes New Faces
quests.hint: Which title covers both the changes and their result?
quests.explanation: The complaints and the café are parts of the story. The visit counts show what the changes accomplished.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title combines the new features with the new audience they attract.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Most people wince when they hear a recording of their own voice. It sounds higher and thinner than the voice they think they have. The reason is that, when we speak, sound travels to our ears both through the air and through the bones of the skull, which adds low tones. A recording captures only the air-borne sound, so it is closer to what everyone else hears.
options: Role of the Skull in Hearing
Why Your Recorded Voice Sounds Strange to You
quests.correctAnswer: Why Your Recorded Voice Sounds Strange to You
quests.hint: The passage opens with a reaction and then supplies a reason. What is being explained?
quests.explanation: Microphones and the skull are pieces of the explanation. The passage's subject is the strangeness people feel and why it happens.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice names the puzzling experience and points to the explanation the passage gives.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Marcos had planned to throw away the old bicycle in the shed. Its chain was rusted and its tires were flat; when his neighbor's daughter asked if she could try to fix it, he shrugged. Two weeks later, she rolled it out with new tires and a bell shaped like a frog. Marcos found himself riding it to the store the next morning, embarrassed at how much he enjoyed it.
options: Giving an Old Bicycle a Second Chance
Buying a Bell for a Bicycle
A Neighbor's Daughter Learning to Ride
quests.correctAnswer: Giving an Old Bicycle a Second Chance
quests.hint: Look at how Marcos feels about the bicycle at the start and at the end.
quests.explanation: The chain and the frog bell are small details. The story is about a discarded object finding new use, and what it brings back for Marcos.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title covers the bicycle's journey from discarded to enjoyed, which is the arc of the story.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In some Mediterranean towns, shops close in the afternoon and streets empty. Visitors often read this as laziness. Locals, however, explain that summer afternoons are too hot for work, so people rest and return in the cooler evening, when the shops reopen until late. The schedule is not an absence of effort but a different arrangement of it.
options: Scheduling the Day Around the Summer Heat
quests.correctAnswer: Scheduling the Day Around the Summer Heat
quests.hint: What explanation do the locals offer, and how does the last sentence use it?
quests.explanation: The closed shops and the visitors' view are the puzzle. The passage's real point is the reasoning behind the schedule.
quests.whyThisTitle: It names the schedule and the cause that the locals give for it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Cheap monthly subscriptions seem harmless. One for music, one for films, one for a fitness app, one for storage. Individually, each costs less than a sandwich. But few people track them, and when a household finally adds them up, it often finds a monthly total comparable to a utility bill, including services nobody has used in months.
options: How Small Subscriptions Add Up Unnoticed
Comparing Music and Film Services Every Month
quests.correctAnswer: How Small Subscriptions Add Up Unnoticed
quests.hint: The passage starts by calling the payments harmless. What changes when they are added together?
quests.explanation: The individual services are examples and the utility bill is a comparison. The passage is about the total that no one notices.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title matches the passage's move from small individual costs to a surprisingly large total.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Asked what the hardest part of her job was, the nurse did not mention long shifts or difficult patients. She spoke instead about the moment after a family leaves the room, when there is a fresh set of patients waiting and no time to feel what has just happened. She has learned to step into the corridor for thirty seconds, take a breath, and then go on. Colleagues tell her they have started doing the same.
options: One Nurse's Way of Coping Between Patients
quests.correctAnswer: One Nurse's Way of Coping Between Patients
quests.hint: Notice what the nurse chooses not to mention. What does she talk about instead?
quests.explanation: Long shifts and hard conversations are what the question might suggest, but she names something else. The passage centers on how she copes with that moment.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title focuses on the brief pause she takes, which the passage says colleagues have adopted.
